L181:     CONSUMER PRICE INDEX - AUGUST 2026
L182:     The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in August
L183:     after rising 0.1 percent in July, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Over the last 12 months, the all
L184:     items index increased 3.4 percent before seasonal adjustment.
L185: 
L186:     The index for gasoline rose 3.9 percent in August, accounting for over one third of the monthly all items increase. The
L187:     index for energy increased 2.1 percent over the month. The shelter index rose 0.3 percent in August after rising 0.1
L188:     percent in July. The index for food increased 0.1 percent over the month, as the index for food away from home increased
L189:     0.3 percent.
L190: 
L191:     The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent after increasing 0.2 percent in July. Indexes that
L192:     increased over the month include communication, lodging away from home, airline fares, education, and used cars and
L193:     trucks. Conversely, the index for medical care and the index for motor vehicle insurance were among the major indexes
L194:     that decreased in August.
L195: 
L196:     The all items index rose 3.4 percent for the 12 months ending August as it did for the 12 months ending July. The all
L197:     items less food and energy index rose 2.4 percent over the year, following a 2.5-percent increase over the 12 months
L198:     ending July. The energy index increased 16.3 percent for the 12 months ending August. The food index increased 2.7
L199:     percent over the last year.

L240:     Food
L241: 
L242:     The food index rose 0.1 percent in August, as it did in July. The index for food at home was unchanged over the month.
L243:     Four of the six major grocery store food group indexes increased in August. The meats, poultry, fish, and eggs index
L244:     increased 0.1 percent over the month, as the eggs index rose 2.9 percent. The index for other food at home also
L245:     increased 0.1 percent in August. The nonalcoholic beverages index increased 0.2 percent over the month, and the dairy
L246:     and related products index rose 0.3 percent. The index for cereals and bakery products was unchanged in August.
L247: 
L248:     In contrast, the fruits and vegetables index declined 0.4 percent in August after falling in the preceding 2 months. The
L249:     index for lettuce continued to fall, declining 6.2 percent in August after decreasing 16.4 percent in July.
L250:     The food away from home index rose 0.3 percent in August. The index for full service meals rose 0.4 percent, and the
L251:     index for limited service meals was unchanged over the month.
L252: 
L253:     The food at home index rose 2.2 percent over the 12 months ending in August. The index for other food at home increased
L254:     2.4 percent, and the index for fruits and vegetables rose 3.2 percent over the year. The nonalcoholic beverages index
L255:     increased 3.7 percent over the 12 months ending in August, and the cereals and bakery products index rose 2.6 percent
L256:     over the same period. The index for meats, poultry, fish, and eggs increased 1.1 percent over the last 12 months. In
L257:     contrast, the dairy and related products index fell 0.3 percent over the year.
L258: 
L259:     The food away from home index rose 3.4 percent over the last year. The index for full service meals rose 3.5 percent,
L260:     and the index for limited service meals rose 3.2 percent over the 12 months ending in August.
L261: 
L262:     Energy
L263: 
L264:     The index for energy increased 2.1 percent in August after falling 1.5 percent in July. The gasoline index increased 3.9
L265:     percent over the month. (Before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices increased 2.5 percent in August.) Conversely, the
L266:     index for natural gas decreased 1.1 percent in August, and the index for electricity fell 0.2 percent.
L267:     The index for energy increased 16.3 percent over the past 12 months due in large part to the index for gasoline rising
L268:     27.4 percent over the same period. The natural gas index increased 4.4 percent over the 12 months ending in August, and
L269:     the electricity index rose 3.8 percent.
L270: 
L271:     All items less food and energy
L272: 
L273:     The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in August after rising 0.2 percent in July. The shelter
L274:     index increased 0.3 percent over the month after rising 0.1 percent in July. The index for owners' equivalent rent rose
L275:     0.2 percent in August as did the index for rent. The lodging away from home index rose 2.4 percent in August after
L276:     falling 2.8 percent the previous month.
L277: 
L278:     The index for communication increased 2.3 percent over the month after rising 0.6 percent in July. The airline fares
L279:     index rose 2.7 percent in August, and the education index increased 0.8 percent. The index for used cars and trucks
L280:     increased 0.4 percent in August, and the index for new vehicles rose 0.3 percent. The personal care index and the
L281:     household furnishings and operations index also increased over the month.
L282: 
L283:     The medical care index decreased 0.2 percent in August after rising 0.4 percent in July. The index for dental services
L284:     fell 0.6 percent over the month. The hospital services index, physicians' services index, and prescription drugs index
L285:     were all unchanged in August.
L286: 
L287:     The motor vehicle insurance index declined 0.8 percent in August after falling 0.3 percent in July. The index for
L288:     apparel was unchanged in August as was the index for recreation.
L289: 
L290:     The index for all items less food and energy rose 2.4 percent over the past 12 months. The shelter index increased 3.0
L291:     percent over the last year. Other indexes with notable increases over the last year include airline fares (+23.4
L292:     percent), recreation (+2.7 percent), medical care (+1.6 percent), and personal care (+3.8 percent).
L293: 
L294:     Not seasonally adjusted CPI measures
L295: 
L296:     The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 3.4 percent over the last 12 months to an index level
L297:     of 334.980 (1982-84=100). For the month, the index rose 0.3 percent prior to seasonal adjustment.
L298:     The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) increased 3.5 percent over the last 12
L299:     months to an index level of 328.481 (1982-84=100). For the month, the index increased 0.4 percent prior to seasonal
L300:     adjustment.
L301: 
L302:     The Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U) increased 3.3 percent over the last 12 months. For
L303:     the month, the index increased 0.3 percent on a not seasonally adjusted basis. Please note that the indexes for the past
L304:     10 to 12 months are subject to revision.

L309:     Technical Note
L310: 
L311:     Brief Explanation of the CPI
L312:     The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
L313:     spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
L314:     The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
L315:     of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
L316:     unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
L317:     spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
L318:     those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
L319:     two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
L320:     All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U).
L321: 
L322:     The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
L323:     included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
L324:     from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
L325:     weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
L326:     population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
L327: 
L328:     The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
L329:     and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
L330:     across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
L331:     supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
L332:     purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
L333:     all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
L334:     geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
L335:     visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
L336: 
L337:     In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
L338:     represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
L339:     a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
L340:     country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
L341:     indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
L342:     for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
L343:     are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
L344:     quarterly revisions.

L346:     The index measures price change from a designed reference date. For most of the CPI-U and the CPI-W, the reference base
L347:     is 1982-84 equals 100. The reference base for the C-CPI-U is December 1999 equals 100. An increase of 7 percent from
L348:     the reference base, for example, is shown as 107.000. Alternatively, that relationship can also be expressed as the
L349:     price of a base period market basket of goods and services rising from $100 to $107.
L350: 
L351:     Sampling Error in the CPI
L352: 
L353:     The CPI is a statistical estimate that is subject to sampling error because it is based upon a sample of retail prices
L354:     and not the complete universe of all prices. BLS calculates and publishes estimates of the 1-month, 2-month, 6-month,
L355:     and 12-month percent change standard errors annually for the CPI-U. These standard error estimates can be used to
L356:     construct confidence intervals for hypothesis testing. For example, the estimated standard error of the 1-month percent
L357:     change is 0.04 percent for the U.S. all items CPI. This means that if we repeatedly sample from the universe of all
L358:     retail prices using the same methodology, and estimate a percentage change for each sample, then 95 percent of these
L359:     estimates will be within 0.08 percent of the 1-month percentage change based on all retail prices. For example, for a
L360:     1-month change of 0.2 percent in the all items CPI-U, we are 95 percent confident that the actual percent change based
L361:     on all retail prices would fall between 0.12 and 0.28 percent. For the latest data, including information on how to use
L362:     the estimates of standard error, see www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/variance-estimates/home.htm.
L363: 
L364:     Calculating Index Changes
L365:     Movements of the indexes from 1 month to another are usually expressed as percent changes rather than changes in index
L366:     points, because index point changes are affected by the level of the index in relation to its base period, while
L367:     percent changes are not. The following table shows an example of using index values to calculate percent changes:
L368: 
L369:                                 Item A                  Item B                      Item C
L370:     Year I                      112.500                 225.000                     110.000
L371:     Year II                     121.500                 243.000                     128.000
L372:     Change in index points      9.000                   18.000                      18.000
L373:     Percent change              9.0/112.500 x 100 = 8.0  18.0/225.000 x 100 = 8.0   18.0/110.000 x 100 = 16.4

L375:     Use of Seasonally Adjusted and Unadjusted Data
L376:     The Consumer Price Index (CPI) program produces both unadjusted and seasonally adjusted data. Seasonally adjusted data
L377:     are computed using seasonal factors derived by the X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal adjustment method. These factors are
L378:     updated each February, and the new factors are used to revise the previous 5 years of seasonally adjusted data. The
L379:     factors are available at www.bls.gov/web/cpi/cpi-seasonal-factors.xlsx. For more information on data revision
L380:     scheduling, please see the Seasonal Adjustment questions and answers page at
L381:     www.bls.gov/cpi/seasonal-adjustment/questions-and-answers.htm and the Timeline of Seasonal Adjustment Methodological
L382:     Changes at www.bls.gov/cpi/seasonal-adjustment/timeline-seasonal-adjustment-methodology-changes.htm.
L383: 
L384:     How to Use Seasonally Adjusted and Unadjusted Data
L385: 
L386:     For analyzing short-term price trends in the economy, seasonally adjusted changes are usually preferred since they
L387:     eliminate the effect of changes that normally occur at the same time and in about the same magnitude every year-such as
L388:     price movements resulting from weather events, production cycles, model changeovers, holidays, and sales. This allows
L389:     data users to focus on changes that are not typical for the time of year.
L390: 
L391:     The unadjusted data are of primary interest to consumers concerned about the prices they actually pay. Unadjusted data
L392:     are also used extensively for escalation purposes. Many collective bargaining contract agreements and pension plans,
L393:     for example, tie compensation changes to the Consumer Price Index before adjustment for seasonal variation. BLS advises
L394:     against the use of seasonally adjusted data in escalation agreements because seasonally adjusted series are revised
L395:     annually for five years.
L396: 
L397:     Intervention Analysis
L398:     The Bureau of Labor Statistics uses intervention analysis seasonal adjustment (IASA) for some CPI series. Sometimes
L399:     extreme values or sharp movements can distort the underlying seasonal pattern of price change. Intervention analysis
L400:     seasonal adjustment is a process by which the distortions caused by such unusual events are estimated and removed from
L401:     the data prior to calculation of seasonal factors. The resulting seasonal factors, which more accurately represent the
L402:     seasonal pattern, are then applied to the unadjusted data.
L403: 
L404:     For example, this procedure was used for the motor fuel series to offset the effects of the 2009 return to normal
L405:     pricing after the worldwide economic downturn in 2008. Retaining this outlier data during seasonal factor calculation
L406:     would distort the computation of the seasonal portion of the time series data for motor fuel, so it was estimated and
L407:     removed from the data prior to seasonal adjustment. Following that, seasonal factors were calculated based on this
L408:     "prior adjusted" data. These seasonal factors represent a clearer picture of the seasonal pattern in the data. The last
L409:     step is for motor fuel seasonal factors to be applied to the unadjusted data.
L410: 
L411:     For the seasonal factors introduced for January 2026, BLS adjusted 57 series using intervention analysis seasonal
L412:     adjustment, including selected food and beverage items, motor fuels and vehicles.
L413: 
L414:     Revision of Seasonally Adjusted Indexes
L415: 
L416:     Seasonally adjusted data, including the U.S. city average all items index levels, are subject to revision for up to 5
L417:     years after their original release. Every year, economists in the CPI calculate new seasonal factors for seasonally
L418:     adjusted series and apply them to the last 5 years of data. Seasonally adjusted indexes beyond the last 5 years of
L419:     data are considered to be final and not subject to revision. For January 2026, revised seasonal factors and seasonally
L420:     adjusted indexes for 2021 to 2025 were calculated and published. For series which are directly adjusted using the
L421:     Census X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal adjustment software, the seasonal factors for 2025 will be applied to data for 2026 to
L422:     produce the seasonally adjusted 2026 indexes. Series which are indirectly seasonally adjusted by summing seasonally
L423:     adjusted component series have seasonal factors which are derived and are therefore not available in advance.
